query: For an FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy protective coating susceptible to progressive plastic deformation during continuous loading, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain its creep resistance? Specify the governing factor and rationale, an unspecified controlled comparison that would reveal it, predicted observations relative to the starting baseline, the operating boundaries under sustained stress, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: The dual-phase microstructure in the FCC/BCC high-entropy alloy protective coating imparts creep resistance by leveraging the high density of incoherent interphase boundaries, which act as obstacles for dislocation motion and delay recovery processes. In particular, the FCC regions accommodate plastic strain (by twinning and limited slip) while the BCC phase deforms mainly via slip, so that their strain‐partitioning and the barrier effect of the FCC/BCC interfaces delay steady-state creep.
generation.material_initial_state: A protective coating with a dual-phase microstructure consisting of 〈001〉-oriented FCC dendrites interpenetrated by a network of BCC (or B2) precipitates/interdendritic regions.
generation.intervention: Tailor the microstructure by processing to create coatings with differing interphase (FCC/BCC) boundary densities (e.g., via adjusted deposition parameters that control dendrite size and precipitate distribution).
generation.conditions: Continuous loading under constant stress at an elevated temperature regime where creep deformation is activated but below the temperature where full recrystallization or phase transformation occurs.
generation.structural_mediator: The density and distribution of FCC/BCC interphase boundaries, which mediate strain partitioning between the ductile FCC and the less-twinnable BCC phase.
generation.mechanism: The interfaces between the FCC and BCC regions act as barriers to dislocation glide and pile-up, thus increasing work hardening and retarding steady-state creep. Additionally, the differential deformation mechanisms (FCC twinning versus BCC slip) create an internal stress field at the boundaries that further impedes dislocation motion and delays the onset of diffusion-assisted creep.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under identical external loading and temperature, coatings with a higher density of FCC/BCC interphase boundaries will exhibit lower creep strain rates and longer creep rupture times compared to coatings with a coarser microstructure (lower boundary density). Compared to the initial (baseline) state, the processed high-boundary-density coating will show reduced steady-state creep deformation.
generation.baseline: A coating having the original as-deposited dual-phase microstructure with moderate interphase boundary density.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to dominate under sustained mechanical stress and elevated temperature conditions where dislocation-mediated deformation is active yet diffusion creep is not fully dominant.
generation.uncertainty: The relative contributions of other mechanisms (e.g., dynamic precipitation, grain boundary sliding, and twinning within the FCC phase) remain to be fully quantified; the extent to which interphase boundary density alone governs the creep behavior may be influenced by compositional variations and local stress states.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of high-entropy alloy protective coating samples with systematically varied FCC/BCC interphase boundary densities by modifying deposition parameters. Subject each sample to constant stress creep tests at a fixed elevated temperature. Use digital image correlation and microstructural characterization (e.g., EBSD/TEM) to measure creep strain rates and observe dislocation structures and interphase boundary evolution over time.
measurements: Creep strain vs. time curves and determination of steady-state creep strain rates
Quantitative microstructural analysis to measure interphase boundary density
Characterization of dislocation activity and strain partitioning between FCC and BCC phases
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If samples with higher FCC/BCC interphase boundary density do not exhibit significantly lower creep strain rates and longer creep lifetimes compared to the baseline, or if variations in boundary density do not correlate with changes in dislocation behavior as predicted, then the hypothesis that interphase boundaries are the dominant factor governing creep resistance is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: One of the most promising applications of FeNiCoCrMoAl-based high-entropy alloy is the fabrication of protective coatings. In this work, gas-atomized powder of FeNiCoCrMo0.5Al1.3 composition was deposited via high-velocity oxygen fuel spraying. It was shown that in-flight oxidation of the powder influences the coating’s phase composition and properties. Powder oxidation and phase transformations were studied under HVOF deposition, and during continuous heating and prolonged isothermal annealing at 800 °C. Optical and scanning electron microscopy observation, energy dispersive X-ray analysis, X-ray diffraction analysis, thermogravimetric analysis, differential thermal analysis, and microhardness tests were used for study. In a gas-atomized state, the powder consisted of BCC supersaturated solid solution. The high rate of heating and cooling and high oxygen concentration during spraying led to oxidation development prior to decomposition of the supersaturated solid solution. Depleted Al layers of BCC transferred to the FCC phase. In this section we present the key experimental observations documenting the stress-strain response of dual-phase FeCoCrNiAl0.5 in relation to its pristine vs. deformed microstructure. After characterizing the undeformed microstructure by EBSD and TEM, the influence of temperature (293K vs. 77K) on the strain-hardening rate is studied and the strain partitioning between fcc and bcc/B2 determined from DIC strain maps. EBSD and (high-resolution) TEM of deformed FeCoCrNiAl0.5 reveal deformation twinning in the fcc phase.

In the present study, the tensile creep tests under constant stress were performed on multiple fine-grained CoCrFeNiMn HEA specimens in the temperature range of 500–600 °C. Specifically, some tests were interrupted at the steady-state stages and cooled quickly to reserve the crept microstructures for examining the microstructural evolution. The objective was to reveal the inherent relationship between microstructural evolution and creep properties of single-phase CoCrFeNiMn high-entropy alloy.
